Management ofPalatally ImpactedMaxillary Canines

Introduction
DefinitionFailure of maxillary canine eruption beyond physiological timing despite complete root development.
Incidence
1–3%
in the general population (2nd most common impaction after 3rd molars).
Distribution
85%
Palatal vs. Buccal
~85% palatal
vs. 15% buccal.
Gender
Female-to-male ratio is 2:1.
92%8%
Laterality
Unilateral (92%) vs. Bilateral (8%)
Clinical SignificanceCritical for canine guidance (mutually protected occlusion) and smile esthetics. Canines are important for facial appearance (lip support), dental function, and smile aesthetics.
Early diagnosis helps prevent complications and makes treatment easier
Clinical Photographs
Palatal viewsIntraoral occlusal photographs of the maxillary arch.
Early Clinical Screening & Red FlagsAges 9–11
Screening Protocol
Target Age: 9–10 years old (mixed dentition).
Bimanual Palpation: Labial vestibule + anterior palate.
Normal Sign: Distinct labial bulge in buccal sulcus.
Golden Rule: Absent labial bulge at age 10+ requires radiographs.
Five Key Clinical Red Flags
1

Asymmetric Eruption: > 6 months delay vs. contralateral canine.

2

Absent Labial Bulge: Flat labial contour above primary canine.

3

Firm Palatal Bulge: Hard, non-tender palatal prominence.

4

Immobile Primary Canine: Retained without mobility past age 12–13.

5

Lateral Incisor Tipping: Distal crown tipping from canine pressure on its root.

PathogenesisWhy Do Canines Deviate Palatally?
The main causes of palatal canine impaction include:
Anomalous Laterals
Lateral incisor root acts as a physical eruption guide. Peg-shaped or missing lateral incisors deprive the canine of guidance.
Result: Crown slips palatally during downward eruption.
Genetic factorsFamily history may increase the risk of canine impaction.
Abnormal tooth positionThe canine may develop in an incorrect direction.
Supernumerary teethExtra teeth may block the eruption path.
Lack of spaceCrowding can prevent the canine from erupting normally.
Abnormal eruption pathThe tooth may move away from its normal position.
Retained deciduous canineThe primary canine may remain and interfere with eruption.
Radiographic Assessment
Radiographs are essential for locating the impacted canine and planning treatment.
Types of radiographs

Periapical views: Show the canine and surrounding tooth roots.

Occlusal views: Help determine whether the canine is located palatally or labially.

Panoramic radiograph (OPG): Gives an overall view of the teeth and jaws.

CBCT: Provides a three-dimensional view when more detailed information is needed.

What do we evaluate?

Position and angulation of the impacted canine.

Relationship with adjacent teeth.

Presence of root resorption.

Depth of impaction.

Presence of associated pathology

Classification of ImpactionTypes I – VII
Radiographic ImagingOPG & CBCT
Treatment Planning
Treatment depends on the position of the canine, patient's age, available space, and the condition of adjacent teeth.
1Observation
Regular follow-up when there are no symptoms or complications.
2Surgical exposure with orthodontic traction
Expose the canine surgically and guide it into the dental arch using orthodontic forces.
3Surgical exposure without traction
Expose the tooth and allow it to erupt naturally in selected cases.
4Extraction
Remove the impacted canine when it cannot be saved or causes serious problems.
5Autotransplantation
Move the canine surgically to another suitable position in the mouth in selected cases.
Indications for Surgery
Surgical treatment may be needed in the following situations:
1

Facilitate orthodontic eruption: Help the impacted canine reach its normal position.

2

Prevent damage to adjacent teeth: Reduce the risk of root resorption of nearby teeth.

3

Associated pathology: Remove or manage cysts and other pathological conditions.

4

Interference with orthodontic treatment: The impacted tooth may prevent proper orthodontic tooth movement.

5

Functional and aesthetic reasons: Restore normal dental function and improve the appearance of the smile

Surgical Techniques
There are two main techniques for surgical exposure.
AOpen Surgical Exposure
  • A palatal flap is raised to expose the impacted canine.
  • A small amount of bone is removed if necessary.
  • The crown of the canine is exposed.
  • The surgical area is left open to allow natural eruption.
  • The patient may need regular follow-up.
BClosed Surgical Exposure
  • A full-thickness flap is raised.
  • Bone is removed carefully to expose the crown.
  • An orthodontic attachment and gold chain are bonded to the canine.
  • The flap is repositioned and sutured.
  • The chain remains accessible for orthodontic traction.

Step-by-Step Surgical Procedure
The main steps of surgical exposure include:
1
Local anesthesiaGive local anesthesia to ensure patient comfort.
2
Incision and flap reflectionMake an incision and raise the palatal flap.
3
Identify the impacted canineLocate the crown of the tooth.
4
Bone removal (osteotomy)Remove a small amount of bone covering the crown.
5
Exposure of crownExpose enough of the crown for attachment placement.
6
Bond orthodontic attachmentAttach a bracket or gold chain when traction is planned.
7
Flap repositioning and suturingReposition the flap according to the selected technique.
8
Postoperative tractionStart orthodontic traction when appropriate.
Orthodontic Traction
Orthodontic traction is used to guide the impacted canine into its correct position.

A gold chain or orthodontic bracket is bonded to the exposed canine.

The attachment is connected to the orthodontic appliance.

Gentle and controlled orthodontic forces are applied.

The canine is gradually moved toward the dental arch.

Regular orthodontic visits are needed to monitor tooth movement.

The force should be controlled to avoid damage to adjacent teeth and supporting tissues.

Main goalTo bring the canine into its normal position while maintaining healthy surrounding tissues
Complications
Possible complications of surgical exposure and orthodontic traction include:
1

Damage to adjacent roots: Root resorption may occur due to close contact or improper movement.

2

Injury to the nasopalatine neurovascular bundle: May cause bleeding or altered sensation.

3

Infection and pain: Can occur after surgery.

4

Attachment failure: The orthodontic bracket or gold chain may become detached.

5

Gingival recession: May affect the appearance of the final result.

6

Ankylosis: The canine becomes fused to the surrounding bone.

7

Failed eruption: The canine may fail to move into its correct position.

Postoperative sutures
Root resorption
Postoperative Care
Good postoperative care helps reduce complications and improve healing.
1

Analgesics: Prescribe painkillers when needed.

2

Oral hygiene instructions: Keep the surgical area clean and avoid traumatic brushing.

3

Chlorhexidine mouth rinse: Use if indicated to help control bacterial plaque.

4

Soft diet: Avoid hard and hot foods during the early healing period.

5

Avoid disturbing the surgical site: Do not touch or irritate the wound.

6

Follow-up visits: Check wound healing and remove sutures when required.

7

Orthodontic follow-up: Monitor the movement of the impacted canine.

Prognosis and Success Factors
The success of treatment depends on several factors:
1Early diagnosis
Early detection allows better treatment planning.
2Favorable position and angulation
A more favorable canine position improves the chance of success.
3Adequate space in the arch
Sufficient space is needed for proper eruption.
4Root development
The stage of root development may influence treatment.
5No ankylosis
An ankylosed canine is difficult to move orthodontically.
6Patient cooperation
Good oral hygiene and regular follow-up improve the outcome.
Summary

Early detection of palatally impacted canines is very important.

Clinical examination and radiographic assessment help determine the position of the canine.

Treatment depends on the patient's condition and the position of the impacted tooth.

Surgical exposure may be performed using open or closed techniques.

Orthodontic traction is commonly used to guide the canine into its normal position.

Preserving the natural canine is preferred whenever possible.

Proper postoperative care and regular follow-up improve treatment success
